idiom_name: opaque types and capability-typed parameters, over JVM framework method security
implementation_notes: Scala 3's opaque types give the in-process half of the rule: the type equality is visible only inside the scope where the alias is defined, so a component can hold a value whose constructor it cannot call and whose representation it cannot see, which is the capability-token idea expressed as a type instead of as a rights table (Scala 2 reaches a similar place with value classes or sealed hierarchies). Effect libraries push it further by making authority part of the signature: with ZIO, an effect can only use the services listed in its environment type, so the authority a component requires is visible in its type rather than in a comment. The enforcing decision on the JVM is the framework's and the container's - Spring Security, Play or Akka HTTP authorization with JSR-250 annotations, inside a non-root process that the container bounds - because the JDK's own permission check is gone: JEP 486 disabled the SecurityManager in Java 24. The classic policy object remains justified where rights are runtime data, such as per-tenant entitlements that no type can express statically.
pitfalls: Opaque types are erased at runtime: Java callers, reflection and anything crossing the JVM boundary see the underlying type, so type-level least privilege is a compile-time discipline rather than a security boundary.

Given or implicit capabilities leak by scope: a token made available as a given can be used anywhere in that scope and by everything it calls, so keep capability givens tightly scoped or pass them explicitly where the authority changes.

Framework annotations only apply where the proxy or interceptor runs, and after JEP 486 the JVM has no permission check to catch the calls it misses - unannotated methods and self-invocations are unsecured by default.
